paras: The killing of an alleged looter in the 1903 Topeka flood was the shooting of an unnamed Black man by a volunteer rescue party from St. Joseph, Missouri, in flooded Topeka, Kansas, in the days before June 3, 1903. The rescuers reported that they had caught him 'in the act of looting deserted houses' and shot him dead. The killing was known only from the rescuers' own report, which a wire dispatch carried to papers across the country and to at least one Black weekly as a sentence in a story about rescued schoolchildren.

Topeka was among the Kansas cities flooded in late May and early June 1903, and St. Joseph sent a party of seventy-five men with steam launches and rowboats to help with rescue work. The Waterbury Evening Democrat placed the flood victims the men had aided at North Topeka.

According to the dispatch, the St. Joseph men took 200 schoolchildren from the Grant School, where they had been trapped since the previous Friday in a 'half-starved condition.' During the same operation, the dispatch stated, 'the rescuers shot and killed a negro caught in the act of looting deserted houses.' The man was not named, the place and time of the shooting were not given, and no version says which of the rescuers fired. The party then returned to St. Joseph with the names of thirty identified dead, and other volunteers took its place.
No report of an inquest, an identification of the dead man or any inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

The item reached white papers as a St. Joseph wire dated June 3, sometimes June 4, and ran from June 4 in New Haven, Waterbury, Savannah, Richmond and St. Paul to June 10 and 11 in South Carolina and New Jersey weeklies. Most printed it under headlines about the rescued children, such as 'Many Were Rescued' and 'School Children Rescued.' Others put the killing itself in the headline: the New Haven Journal and Courier ran the deck 'Negro Killed for Looting,' the Keowee Courier '200 Children Rescued and a Negro Killed,' and the Waterbury paper 'A Negro Looter Meets His Death While Pillaging,' wording that presented the accusation as fact. The Richmond Times Dispatch's version said the man was caught 'robbing' rather than looting the houses.

In the Black press the Baltimore Afro-American carried the story on June 6 under '200 Little Prisoners,' the same text the Bridgeton Pioneer used, and repeated the sentence on the shooting without comment. Like the white papers, it identified the dead man only by race and gave the rescuers' account as the whole of the story.

Every version gives a single death at Topeka; a report of seven Black men shot on a raft while looting, sometimes associated with this case, came from East St. Louis, Illinois, a week later and was itself described as unconfirmed.

reader.title: Killing of an alleged looter in the 1903 Topeka flood
bases: An armed volunteer party (75 men sent from St. Joseph, Mo., to do rescue work) reported that it shot and killed a Black man it said it caught looting deserted houses in flooded Topeka; no officers, arrest or crowd is mentioned (A5, A12, A10).

Every report (A1-A5, A10, A12, A13, A15) is the same St. Joseph wire, which relays the rescuers' own account; no Topeka paper, official or second witness confirms it, and the Topeka Plaindealer's flood coverage (A7-A9) does not mention it.

accounts.label: St. Joseph rescuers' report (wire)
accounts.gist: The returning St. Joseph rescue party reported that, besides saving 200 schoolchildren from the Grant School, it shot and killed a Black man caught looting deserted houses. The account comes only from the party that did the shooting.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire under rescue headlines ('Many Were Rescued', 'School Children Rescued'); the New Haven, Waterbury and Keowee papers put the killing in the headline or deck, Waterbury as 'A Negro Looter Meets His Death While Pillaging', treating the looting as fact.
The Baltimore Afro-American printed the same text as the Bridgeton Pioneer under '200 Little Prisoners', with no comment on the shooting.

conflicts.note: The record's alternative count of 7 comes from an unconfirmed East St. Louis report of seven Black men shot on a raft (A14, A16, A17), a separate episode; no Topeka source gives more than one.
